title: Other Christians
hook: Methodists, Baptists, Pentecostals and others in dialogue with Catholics

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lutherans and Catholics in Lund: thanksgiving, repentance and commitment. Your line was from conflict to communion. Did you tell someone's side of an argument fairly before your own? Day one thousand four hundred twenty.

A Saturday morning on a main street. A Methodist church with a sign out front about a pancake breakfast. A Baptist church with a baptism pool behind the pulpit. A storefront Pentecostal church where the singing spills out onto the sidewalk. A Catholic parish with confessions until noon. Four doors, four ways of worshiping, and Catholics walking past all of them. What does the Catholic Church say about the people behind those other doors? Today, other Christians.
screen: `FOUR DOORS ON ONE STREET.` → `FOUR WAYS OF WORSHIPING.` → `WHO IS BEHIND THE OTHER DOORS?`

segments.voice: First, what the council said. The decree on ecumenism teaches that those who believe in Christ and have been properly baptized are in a real, though imperfect, communion with the Catholic Church. It says they are rightly called Christians, and rightly accepted by Catholics as brothers in the Lord. Brothers is the council's word. Second, why baptism matters so much here. In the Douay-Rheims, Paul writes to the Ephesians: "One Lord, one faith, one baptism." The Catholic Church recognizes baptism given with water in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit in other churches. So a Catholic and a Baptist, whatever they disagree about, are already joined by one baptism. Third, the conversations. Beyond Anglicans and Lutherans, the Catholic Church holds formal dialogues with Methodists, with Baptists, with Pentecostals and with others. Some are old, some newer. They talk about grace, Scripture, the Spirit, holiness and mission. Methodists bring their founder John Wesley, who once preached that even when Christians can't think alike, they might still love alike. Pentecostals bring their experience of the Spirit, which the Catholic charismatic renewal also prizes. Last, honesty. These dialogues don't erase real differences: about the sacraments, the pope, Mary, how churches are led. They name them. But the starting point isn't suspicion. It's a family resemblance, one baptism, one Lord, and the council's word: brothers.
screen: `A REAL, THOUGH IMPERFECT, COMMUNION.` · `ONE LORD, ONE FAITH, ONE BAPTISM.` · `METHODISTS, BAPTISTS, PENTECOSTALS.` · `DIFFERENCES NAMED, NOT ERASED.` · then, large: `BROTHERS IN THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Settle, and breathe. Think of one Christian tradition you know little about: Methodist, Baptist, Pentecostal, Mennonite, Orthodox, any one. Picture one of their churches and the people walking into it this Sunday. If you pray, you can pray for them as the council describes them, as brothers and sisters in Christ. If you don't, hold them in mind with goodwill and a little curiosity. After the bell, learn one thing about that tradition from its own people: its own website, a hymn, a friend. The bell holds the time.
Other Christians. Baptized believers in Christ in other churches, whom the council calls brothers in the Lord. Today's word.
Your line: brothers and sisters in Christ. Today, when you pass a church that isn't yours, give it a nod, the way you'd nod to a cousin across the street. Day one thousand four hundred twenty.

howItsDone: The Catholic Church holds official dialogues with a number of Christian communities, including Methodists, Baptists and Pentecostals, and in some towns local churches of different traditions share prayer services and service projects.

original.note: Greek, brothers: the word Paul's letters use for fellow believers, sisters included.

notes: Unitatis Redintegratio 3 paraphrased: those who believe in Christ and have been truly (properly) baptized are in communion with the Catholic Church even though this communion is imperfect; justified by faith in baptism, they are incorporated into Christ; they have a right to be called Christians and are accepted as brothers by the children of the Catholic Church.
